adrian_b · Nov 7, 2026

There are some claims of deciphering some parts of the Linear A Minoan documents, which are not corroborated yet by other researchers, but which are nonetheless more plausible than all the earlier claims of deciphering Linear A, which were definitely wrong.

If this partial decipherment were right, the language of Linear A would be Hurrian, i.e. the language of a state that was important around 4 thousand years ago and which was located in the territory of present Syria.

The Hurrians from Syria also used writing, but there they had adapted a variant of the cuneiform writing. Some Hurrian texts have also been found written with the Semitic alphabet used in Ugarit. There are some features of the Hittite variant of cuneiform writing that seem to have been taken from their Southern neighbors, the Hurrians, so it is possible that the Hittites have learned writing from the Hurrians, who had been using cuneiform writing for a few centuries before the Hittites, instead of taking writing directly from Assyria. This would be similar to how the Greek users of Linear B have taken writing from the Minoan users of Linear A.

It seems that the Hurrians had a rich mythology, which influenced many of their neighbors, and a few of their myths have been preserved, inclusively in the Hittite archives.

There exists no certain relationship between Hurrian and any language that survives today. In the antiquity there was a related language spoken in Urartu, on the territory of present Armenia. There are however a few similarities between Hurrian and some of the languages of the Caucasus area, but due to the difference in time of many thousands of years it cannot be known whether there is any genetic connection between them.

So if the claims about a decipherment of Linear A were true, that would imply that the Minoans have colonized Crete, and probably also Cyprus, by coming from the nearby territory where today is Syria. This sounds plausible, and that territory is one that had become "civilized" before the more Northern territories of Anatolia and Greece.

What a coincidence that I visited the Akrotiri ruins only a few weeks ago. It was truly remarkable. Unlike Pompeii, the people of ancient Thera appear to have been familiar enough with volcanoes to know to evacuate well ahead of the eruption. No remains of valuables, pets, or humans have been discovered at the site. Still, much about the life and culture of these people is able to be learned from their architecture, visual culture, and more. The remains of Linear A tablets and frescos have strongly associated it with Minoan civilization (though the guide we had at the site was careful to not to simply call the people “Minoans”).

antman · Nov 7, 2026

They had no defensive walls, at least not in the way we might expect, and no coinage. Still, they managed to maintain extensive trade networks, with connections reaching as far as Central Asia, and materials such as lapis lazuli ultimately originating in what is now Afghanistan.

The Aegean Sea around 1600 BC was probably far busier than we tend to imagine, with substantial maritime trade connecting islands, coastal settlements, and distant civilizations. Without compasses, sailors relied on landmarks, celestial navigation, experience, and routes that often took them from island to island. Minoan settlements across the Aegean may have helped secure maritime routes and provided a degree of protection to Crete itself. This could partly explain why major Minoan palaces lacked the defensive fortifications common elsewhere. There is also another issue, one that receives less attention in popular accounts, despite having affected several Eastern Mediterranean societies of the period.

The eruption of Thera was approaching, and there is archaeological evidence suggesting that at least some inhabitants had time to leave before the final catastrophic event. The absence of human remains in the excavated areas of Akrotiri is particularly striking, although it does not establish that the entire island was successfully evacuated. Some evidence also suggests limited human activity or resettlement in the broader area after the eruption.

The Minoans were not immediately destroyed by the eruption. Its impact on their fleets, ports, and trading networks remains debated, but the disruption may have weakened their maritime position. Over the following centuries, several major Minoan palaces were destroyed, in circumstances that likely involved a combination of natural disasters, conflict, and political change. Some destruction layers suggest deliberate burning, although the precise events and motivations remain uncertain. At one palace, evidence of exceptionally intense fire has prompted interpretations involving stored combustible materials and restricted ventilation, potentially producing furnace-like temperatures. The exact mechanism, however, is not firmly established.

The changing balance of power in the Aegean eventually favored the Mycenaeans, who came to dominate much of the region. Centuries later, the wider Eastern Mediterranean experienced another series of upheavals, conventionally associated with the Late Bronze Age collapse and the groups described in Egyptian records as the Sea Peoples. These events were separated by considerable time, and their causes were probably more complex than a single chain of disasters or conquests.

And that is perhaps the more important story of what was lost. Long-distance trade networks were disrupted or reorganized. In parts of the Aegean, palace administration disappeared, along with the use of Linear B writing. Monumental construction and certain specialized techniques declined or changed, although this did not mean that mathematical or architectural knowledge vanished everywhere. Earlier artifacts such as the Phaistos Disc, with its repeated stamped symbols, remind us that these societies had developed sophisticated techniques whose full significance we still do not understand.

Some regions also experienced declining use of wheeled transport, possibly reflecting changes in infrastructure, terrain, economics, and social organization rather than a literal forgetting of the wheel. Population losses, displacement, and settlement abandonment were substantial in some areas, but their scale varied across the Eastern Mediterranean.

By around the eighth century BC, alphabetic writing had become established in Greece, following centuries without the earlier palace-based writing system. Settlement patterns had changed, and some communities had moved to more defensible locations. Memories of earlier events may have survived through oral traditions and legends, although connecting individual myths to particular historical disasters is inherently speculative.

That centuries-long disruption in technology, trade, and social organization may have had consequences extending far beyond its immediate aftermath. Technological progress is not necessarily linear, and the loss of complex networks can affect development for generations. The cumulative effect is difficult to measure, but potentially enormous.

To make a very broad and deliberately speculative analogy, perhaps AI could have been invented in 1400 AD under a radically different historical trajectory, and by now we might all be virtual.

On another note, all wtitten from memory, not an archeologist but I assisted the team that worked on the computational reconstruction of the Thera frescoes, which are now on display. The dedication of the Greek archaeological team was legendary in its own right.
